title: Crowned Buddha

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Purchase, Friends of Asian Art Gifts, 1986
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A large wooden sculpture of the Buddha wearing a crown, finished with lacquer and gold. It is taller than most adults, about 172 centimeters, and has a golden, glowing surface.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record (title, date, medium, culture, classification, tags Buddhism, Buddha, Crowns, public-domain flag, image URLs, credit line) and the Met catalog page (period and dimensions)

context: A wooden statue of the Buddha wearing a crown, made in Burma during the Pagan period, around the 13th to early 14th century. It is finished with lacquer and gilding and stands about 172 cm (5 feet 8 inches) tall. The Met's record does not give label text about its pose or original setting.

descriptions.k: This big golden statue is the Buddha. He is wearing a crown! The statue is made of wood and covered in shiny gold. It is as tall as a grown-up. Why do you think the Buddha has a crown here?
descriptions.g12: This Buddha statue from Burma is as tall as a grown-up. It is made of wood, with lacquer and shiny gold. The Buddha wears a crown, which is not common in every Buddha statue. What do you think a crown tells us? How does the gold make the statue feel?
descriptions.g35: Made in Burma more than 700 years ago, this wooden Buddha is nearly 1.7 meters tall. Artists covered it in lacquer, a hard, shiny coating from tree sap, and then added gold. The Buddha wears a crown, which is different from many simpler images. Why might artists show a spiritual teacher with a royal crown? What does the gold add?
descriptions.g68: Carved from wood and finished with lacquer and gilt, this Crowned Buddha was made in Burma during the Pagan period, around the 13th to early 14th century. At about 172 cm tall, it is life-size. A crown on a Buddha combines ideas of spiritual and royal greatness, a pairing found in Southeast Asian Buddhist art. How do size, gold, and crown shape the way a viewer approaches the figure?
descriptions.g910: This Pagan-period sculpture of a crowned Buddha, in wood with lacquer and gilt, stands about 172 cm tall. Crowned Buddha images are found in Southeast Asian art and join the Buddha's spiritual authority with the imagery of kingship, though interpretations vary. Gilding makes the figure radiant, and wood and lacquer show a different tradition from stone or bronze. How do material, scale, and royal attributes work together to create presence, and what remains uncertain?
descriptions.g1112: A crowned Buddha raises intriguing questions of iconography: why would a figure associated with renunciation wear royal regalia? Scholars offer several explanations, and the Met's record for this wooden, lacquered, and gilded Pagan-period work gives few specifics. The life-size scale (about 172 cm), the glowing gilded surface, and the choice of wood invite reflection on materials, patronage, and ritual use. Consider how a museum setting changes the experience of an image once made to be venerated.

k.daily: This Buddha wears a crown. What does a crown make you think of?
k.emotion: Does the statue look calm, angry, or sleepy? Show us the face you see.
k.observation: Find the crown on the Buddha. What else do you see on the statue?
k.analysis: Where do your eyes go first on this tall statue? Why do you think so?
k.line: Run your finger from the top of the crown down the whole statue. What kind of line does it make?
k.shape: Look at the crown. What shapes can you see in it?
k.color: The statue is gold. What other things do you know that are gold?
k.texture: The statue is made of wood with a shiny coating. How do you think it would feel?
k.space: This statue is about as tall as a grown-up. How would you feel standing next to it?
k.light: Gold shines when light hits it. Where does the statue look the shiniest?
k.meaning: A crown can mean a king. Why might someone put a crown on the Buddha?
k.culture: People in Burma made this statue more than 700 years ago. Where do you think they put it?
k.technique: This statue is carved from wood. What tools might the maker have used?
k.personal: If you could wear a crown for a day, what would you do?
k.critical: The statue is very old. What do you think has stayed the same, and what might have changed?

g12.daily: The Buddha wears a crown on this statue. What do you think the crown is telling us?
g12.emotion: How does the golden color make you feel about this statue: calm, joyful, or serious? Why?
g12.observation: List five things you see on the statue, from the crown to the base.
g12.analysis: How does the artist lead your eyes from the crown down along the figure?
g12.line: Find tall, straight lines in the statue. How do they make it feel steady?
g12.shape: Look at the shape of the crown at the top of the statue. How does that shape help your eyes move up?
g12.color: Gold and brown are the main colors. How do they work together to make the statue feel rich?
g12.texture: The statue is wood covered in lacquer and gold. Which parts might feel smooth and which might feel bumpy?
g12.space: The statue is about 172 centimeters tall. How is it like standing next to a real person?
g12.light: Gold can seem to glow. Where would a candle or sunlight make the statue sparkle?
g12.meaning: Kings wear crowns, and the Buddha is a spiritual teacher. Why might an artist combine them?
g12.culture: This statue was made in Burma in a time called the Pagan period. What can an old statue tell us about people long ago?
g12.technique: The maker carved wood, covered it with lacquer, and added gold. Why might the maker choose these layers?
g12.personal: What object in your life feels very special to you? How do you treat it?
g12.critical: This statue was made to be respected. How can we look at it carefully and still be respectful?

g35.daily: What do the crown, the gold, and the size of this Buddha tell you about how people saw him?
g35.emotion: How does the glow of gold change the feeling of the statue compared with plain wood?
g35.observation: Take one minute to look for details of the crown, face, and clothing. What did you notice last?
g35.analysis: How does the sculptor use the crown and the tall shape to focus attention at the top of the statue?
g35.line: How do vertical lines in the body compare with the lines in the crown?
g35.shape: Which shapes are repeated in the crown and the statue? How do they create unity?
g35.color: Why might artists choose gold for an image of the Buddha? What does it make you think of?
g35.texture: Lacquer is a hard, glossy layer. How would the surface feel different from plain carved wood?
g35.space: The statue is nearly 1.7 meters tall. How does life-size scale change how you relate to a sculpture?
g35.light: How might gold surfaces look different in a dark temple lit by lamps versus in a bright gallery?
g35.meaning: Why might artists show a spiritual teacher wearing a royal crown? What ideas might they be joining?
g35.culture: This statue comes from the Pagan period in Burma. What does a large, carefully finished statue suggest about the importance of Buddhism then?
g35.technique: Wood, lacquer, and gilding are all used here. Why might wood be easier to carve than stone, and what protects it?
g35.personal: Have you ever seen a statue or monument that made you feel small or respectful? What about it did that?
g35.critical: The statue is wood, a material that can decay. What does its survival for centuries tell us about how it was cared for?

g68.daily: How does the combination of crown, gold surface, and human scale shape the way viewers might have experienced this Buddha?
g68.emotion: What mood do gilding and royal ornament give the figure, and how would it change if the Buddha had no crown?
g68.observation: Catalog the visible parts of the figure from crown to base. Which seem most elaborately made?
g68.analysis: How does the sculptor organize the figure to direct attention toward the head and crown?
g68.line: How do long, vertical lines give the figure dignity, and where do details of the crown add decoration?
g68.shape: How does the shape of the crown relate to the figure's overall silhouette?
g68.color: How does gilding unify the figure and communicate value and holiness?
g68.texture: How do lacquer and gilt change the way wood looks and feels compared with raw carving?
g68.space: How does a life-size scale affect your relationship with the figure compared with a small statue?
g68.light: How do gilded surfaces respond to light, and why might that matter for a figure used in worship?
g68.meaning: A crown can signal royal greatness. What different explanations can you offer for placing one on the Buddha?
g68.culture: The statue dates to the Pagan period. What might its materials and scale suggest about the support Buddhism received at the time?
g68.technique: What are the benefits and the risks of making a large Buddha out of wood, lacquer, and gilt?
g68.personal: What does it mean to treat an object with respect, and how do you know when something calls for that?
g68.critical: Which parts of this figure's meaning can we know from looking, and which require outside knowledge of Buddhist art?

g910.daily: How do crown, gilded surface, and scale work together to present the Buddha as both spiritual and regal?
g910.emotion: How does the sculpture establish dignity and serenity through proportion and finish rather than through dramatic expression?
g910.observation: Describe the visual hierarchy of the figure, identifying which features attract attention first and which devices produce that effect.
g910.analysis: How does the vertical structure of the figure support its function as an object of reverence?
g910.line: How does the crown's linear articulation contrast with the continuous contour of the body?
g910.shape: How do the figure's silhouette and the form of the crown together create an upward emphasis?
g910.color: How does gilding transform wood into a radiant surface, and what is conveyed by the choice of gold?
g910.texture: How do lacquer layers and gilding alter the tactile and visual effect of carved wood?
g910.space: How does the near life-size scale shape the viewer's bodily relation to the sculpture in a devotional setting?
g910.light: How might lamp light and gilding have combined to create an atmosphere of radiance in a temple?
g910.meaning: How do scholars explain crowned Buddhas, and why is a single definitive explanation hard to claim?
g910.culture: How does a large wooden image from Pagan-period Burma reflect the importance of Buddhist patronage in the region?
g910.technique: What does the use of wood, lacquer, and gilt reveal about local materials, craft traditions, and the challenges of preservation?
g910.personal: How does encountering a sacred image in a museum differ from encountering it in a place of worship, from your perspective?
g910.critical: What responsibilities do museums have in presenting a sacred object that was made for veneration?

g1112.daily: What interpretive claims does the combination of Buddha and crown support, and where do they exceed the evidence of this single object?
g1112.emotion: How does the sculpture generate reverence through scale, finish, and symmetry, and how might that differ across viewers?
g1112.observation: Describe the sculpture's formal and material construction precisely. Where does description depend on iconographic knowledge?
g1112.analysis: Analyze how verticality, ornament, and gilding structure the sculpture's presentation of authority.
g1112.line: How do contour and ornamental line in the crown negotiate between austerity and splendor?
g1112.shape: How does the figure's silhouette, capped by the crown, contribute to a reading of the Buddha as universal ruler or something else?
g1112.color: How does gilding signify and enact radiance, and how might loss or restoration of gilt alter our understanding?
g1112.texture: How do lacquer and gilt construct a surface that is both protective and symbolic, and what does that imply about the value of the image?
g1112.space: How does life-size scale shape ritual and viewer relations, and what changes when the work is placed in a gallery?
g1112.light: In what ways might the light conditions of a temple have activated the figure's gilded surface, and how can we reconstruct that experience?
g1112.meaning: How should interpreters weigh competing explanations for crowned Buddhas, such as kingship, cosmic authority, or narrative references, in the absence of firm documentation?
g1112.culture: How does a Pagan-period wooden sculpture complicate assumptions that Southeast Asian Buddhist art is mostly known through stone and bronze?
g1112.technique: What does the survival of a lacquered and gilded wooden figure imply about conservation, climate, and the history of its care?
g1112.personal: How do your own beliefs and background shape the way you look at a sacred image from another tradition?
g1112.critical: How should we balance scholarly curiosity with respect for the religious function of an object like this?

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Title, classification (Sculpture), medium, culture, and tags (Buddhism, Buddha, Crowns) checked against the museum record. The catalog page offers no label text, so descriptions rely on the title, materials, size, and general Buddhist iconography. A robed or ornamented figure is assumed from convention; bare-chested depiction could not be ruled out from metadata alone, so descriptions avoid body detail.

teacherNote.context: A near life-size wooden Buddha wearing a crown, finished with lacquer and gilt, from Burma's Pagan period (ca. 13th-early 14th century). The Met record lists its height as about 172 cm.
directions: Ask students to discuss why artists might combine symbols of kingship and spiritual teaching.
Have students compare their height to 172 cm and discuss how life-size scale affects the viewer's response.
Discuss how materials such as wood, lacquer, and gold shape what an image communicates.
